cases.cv_summary: Junior backend developer, one year on a Node.js order service.
cases.jd_summary: Backend engineer, Node.js APIs, SQL performance work.

turns.question: Tell me about a production API problem you debugged.
turns.answer: When our orders API started returning 500s under load, I was responsible for finding the cause. I checked the logs, reproduced it locally, and found a missing database index. I added the index and as a result latency dropped by 40%.

turns.question: And if the index had not fixed it, what would your next steps have been?
turns.answer: If the index had not fixed it, I would profile the query plan with EXPLAIN and check connection pool exhaustion. Last time I did that kind of tuning we cut p95 latency from 900ms to 200ms.

cases.cv_summary: AI application engineer, two years building retrieval-augmented features.
cases.jd_summary: AI engineer for a RAG product: retrieval quality, hallucination control, eval.

turns.question: How did you keep the RAG feature from hallucinating?
turns.answer: I built the retrieval pipeline with pgvector and chunked documents at 500 tokens. In our eval set we cut hallucinated answers by half, and the tradeoff was higher latency on long queries.

turns.question: Push on that: what still gets through the grounding check?
turns.answer: For hallucinations specifically, I added a grounding check that rejects answers with no citation, and we log every rejected answer so we can tune the retriever. The failure mode left is stale documents, so we now re-embed the corpus nightly.

turns.question: What is the retrieval tradeoff you watch most?
turns.answer: The main tradeoff I keep in mind is recall versus precision in the retriever; when we tightened filters we improved precision but lost coverage on edge cases, so I keep an eval set to catch that regression.

cases.cv_summary: QA automation engineer, three years, owns a CI test suite.
cases.jd_summary: QA automation: stabilize CI, flaky test strategy, reporting.

turns.question: Your nightly suite starts flaking. Walk me through what you do.
turns.answer: When our nightly suite went flaky, I quarantined the flaky specs first, added retries only for network-bound tests, and put the flake rate on a dashboard. Over two sprints we reduced the flake rate from 8 percent to 1 percent.

turns.question: What is the downside of retries, and how do you keep them honest?
turns.answer: The tradeoff with retries is that they can hide real race conditions, so I only retry tests that fail on network timeouts, and every retried pass is still reported so we do not lose the signal.

turns.question: How would you compute a running total per customer?

cases.cv_summary: Senior backend engineer, event-driven systems at scale.
cases.jd_summary: Senior backend: Kafka pipelines, delivery semantics, throughput.

turns.question: Walk me through the delivery semantics you chose for your event pipeline.
turns.answer: I designed the event pipeline on Kafka and chose at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers, because exactly-once semantics would have cost too much throughput for our workload. We handle about 50k requests per minute and duplicate incidents went to zero after we shipped the idempotency keys.

turns.question: Last one before we wrap: what would you do differently?
turns.answer: Looking back, the main thing I would improve is the replay tooling; when we needed to reprocess a day of events we had to write ad-hoc scripts, so I would invest in a proper replay service with idempotency guarantees end to end.

cases.cv_summary: Mid backend engineer, owns an orders service on Postgres.
cases.jd_summary: Backend engineer: production ownership, incident response, SQL performance.

turns.question: Picture a real incident: order latency just spiked in production and users are affected. What do you do first?
turns.answer: First I would check the error rate and the logs for the orders service, confirm the blast radius, and roll back the last deploy if the spike lines up with it.

turns.question: The rollback did not help — the logs show timeouts. What now?
turns.answer: The logs show timeouts to the database, so I would check the connection pool metrics and the active query count, and look for a lock or a slow query that started around the deploy.

turns.question: You find one query scanning a full table. Close it out.
turns.answer: Root cause was a missing index after the migration. I added the index back, latency went from 900ms to 120ms, and I wrote a post-incident note so migrations get a query-plan check in CI.

cases.cv_summary: Junior fullstack developer, mostly REST experience, reads about GraphQL.

turns.question: What is your experience with GraphQL?

turns.question: So hands-on: have you actually run a GraphQL server yourself?
turns.answer: Mostly reading, yes. At my last job the API team owned GraphQL so I never touched the resolvers myself.

turns.question: How did you speed up the reporting endpoints?

turns.question: How is that Redis cache invalidated exactly?
turns.answer: The Kafka consumer listens to the write topic and deletes the affected Redis cache keys, and I set the TTL as a safety net in case an event is lost.

turns.question: Which part of that was your call?
turns.answer: I made the call to put invalidation on the write path, and I wrote the consumer myself. I owned the rollout and I handled the duplicate messages we hit in production the first week.
